analysis.one_liner: Rewrites pesticide food-safety rules around a 'negligible risk' standard and blocks states from setting stricter residue limits.
analysis.headline: Backed by 226 House members from both parties, the bill died in committee without ever getting a House floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how the EPA sets limits on pesticide residues in food. It replaces the old rule that banned cancer-causing pesticide residues in processed food with a 'negligible risk' standard, and it lets the EPA allow higher-than-negligible risk if banning the pesticide would hurt the food supply or farm economy. It also stops states from enforcing their own stricter residue limits or warning requirements, and layers new procedures—including validated test evidence, scientific peer review, notice to pesticide makers, and months of comment periods—before the EPA can cancel a pesticide registration.
analysis.who_benefits: Pesticide manufacturers, food processors, and large growers would gain the most: one national tolerance standard instead of a patchwork of state rules, protection from state warning requirements and stricter limits, and a heavy procedural gauntlet before the EPA could pull a dangerous pesticide off the market. Consumers would get some real benefits—a health-based tolerance standard, $12 million more for monitoring residues in imported and domestic food, and new federal investment in pest-control methods that reduce pesticide use—but they would lose the stronger protections the bill replaces.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pesticide makers, food processors, and growers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to revoke any pesticide tolerance set above a level it determines is adequate to protect public health, replacing standards that treated raw and processed foods differently.
Authorizes an additional $12 million for monitoring pesticide residues in both imported and domestic food.

Directs the Agriculture Department to collect pesticide-use data and to research and spread pest-control methods that let farmers reduce or eliminate pesticides posing more than a negligible dietary risk.
Updates the legal definition of adulterated food to cover pesticide residues in processed foods and residue degradation products, closing gaps in the older law.

analysis.who_pays: Food consumers would bear the cost of weaker protections: the bill abandons the zero-cancer-risk rule for pesticide residues in processed food and allows tolerances above negligible risk for farm-economy reasons, and it takes away states' power to enforce stricter limits or require warnings—protections consumers in stricter states currently have. State governments would lose regulatory authority they now hold.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows the EPA to set a tolerance above a negligible dietary risk if the pesticide protects against bigger risks, replaces a riskier pesticide, or if its unavailability would reduce the supply of an adequate, wholesome, and economical food supply—a risk-benefit trade-off that weighs consumer safety against agricultural output.

It preempts state and local pesticide residue limits unless they are identical to the federal standard, and even bars states from requiring warning labels about pesticide residues in food, wiping out tougher protections in states that chose to go further.

The EPA could not even begin the process of canceling a pesticide's registration without a validated test or other significant evidence raising prudent concerns, plus internal peer review, 30 days' notice to the registrant, a 60-day advance notice, and a 90-day comment period—add months of delay before any dangerous pesticide could be restricted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would modernize a badly outdated regulatory structure, and the health-based tolerance standard, monitoring money, and integrated pest management research are genuine gains for consumers. But the core trade runs the other way: the industries that would live under these rules get uniformity, preemption of stricter state laws, and procedural walls around cancellation, while consumers give up the strictest existing protection and the ability of states to protect them independently. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the people most exposed to pesticide residues come out of this bill with less protection in some important situations than they had before.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees for over a year, was approved by a subcommittee and sent to the full Agriculture Committee in July 1994, but the full committee never voted and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Lehman introduced the bill on April 1, 1993, and it was referred jointly to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees.
It attracted 226 cosponsors—144 Republicans and 82 Democrats—unusual bipartisan breadth for a bill rewriting food-safety law.

Subcommittees held a hearing in August 1993 and on July 27, 1994, the Department Operations and Nutrition Subcommittee approved an amended version and forwarded it to the full Agriculture Committee by voice vote.
Neither full committee ever reported the bill, and the House never voted on it; it died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food consumers and state governments are better off that the bill died: they kept the stricter residue rules and state enforcement powers the bill would have replaced, and the pesticide and food-processing industries did not obtain the national preemption and cancellation barriers it offered them.

for.name: Rep. Richard Lehman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 1, 1993, delivered introductory remarks, and made a second floor statement in March 1994 urging action.

for.name: 144 of 176 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, providing the majority of its 226 supporters.

for.name: Agricultural and food-industry groups
for.role: Industry coalition backing uniform pesticide standards
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported the bill's approach of replacing the strict Delaney rule with a negligible-risk standard and national uniformity.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Full committee, chaired by Rep. Kika de la Garza (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a full-committee markup or reported the bill after the subcommittee forwarded it in July 1994.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Full committee, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill beyond referring it to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee in April 1993.

against.name: Consumer and environmental health groups
against.role: Public-interest organizations including natural-resources and food-safety advocates
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a weakening of the Delaney zero-cancer-risk rule and of state authority over pesticide residues.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split across both parties—144 of 176 House Republicans and 82 of 258 House Democrats signed on—and the bill's failure came from committee inaction, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would give registrants 30 days' notice before any cancellation proceeding, require validated test evidence before the EPA could even start a rulemaking, and mandate comment periods lasting months—making it far harder and slower to remove a pesticide from the market. Uniform national tolerances would also eliminate the risk of state-by-state bans.

industries.industry: Food processors, growers, and produce shippers
industries.note: National uniformity would end the patchwork of state residue limits and warning-label requirements, and the EPA would have to weigh effects on food supply and prices before restricting a pesticide. The cost falls on consumers in states with stricter standards, who would lose those protections.

Growers would benefit from required USDA economic-impact analyses before pesticide restrictions, protection for residues from lawful applications, and new federal research into integrated pest management. Some could lose pesticides deemed to pose more than negligible dietary risk, though the bill's exceptions soften that risk.

The bill authorizes $12 million more in government monitoring of residues in imported and domestic food and requires new detection methods for every tolerance, expanding demand for testing work. This serves public health directly.
